text: Every SIEM ships with a library of pre-built, out-of-the-box correlation rules covering common attack patterns. It's tempting to just turn all of them on and call detection coverage done. This lesson covers why that's a real anti-pattern, and what use-case development — the deliberate alternative — actually looks like in practice.

Most pre-built rules were written for a generic environment, not yours, so plenty of them end up irrelevant to your actual log sources, noisy against your normal traffic, or silent on the specific risks your organization actually faces. Use-case development starts from a specific threat or risk the organization cares about, then builds, or selects and tunes, the exact log sources and correlation logic needed to catch it.

Take lateral movement — an attacker who has already landed on one machine moving to additional machines inside the network — as a worked example. An attacker moving laterally typically authenticates to new hosts using credentials harvested from the first one, so the real signal lives in authentication events across every host, correlated together, not in firewall or antivirus logs.

The pattern to look for is the same user account authenticating to an unusual number of distinct hosts within a short time window, more and faster than that account's normal day-to-day behavior. Written as correlation logic: group by user account, count distinct destination hosts authenticated to within one hour, then alert if that count crosses a threshold set above that account's real baseline, not an arbitrary guess.

A generic 'excessive authentication' rule might already exist in the SIEM by default, but without this deliberate process behind it, nobody would know whether its threshold matches this organization's real baseline, whether it's watching the right log sources, or whether it needs the same tuning work from Lesson 15 before it's trustworthy. Use-case development is what turns a SIEM from a tool with a lot of rules in it into an actual, organization-specific detection capability.

That closes out correlation rules and alert logic. Chapter 5 picks up with the real alert triage process — what an analyst actually does once a rule like this one fires and lands an alert in the queue.
